title: Central Ohio families near nuclear plant would benefit from new bill - NewsBreak
text:
By Gracie Collins ,
5 hours ago
PORTSMOUTH, Ohio ( WCMH ) — Relief could be coming to the Pike County families impacted by the Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion plant.
A bipartisan bill was introduced in Congress to expand eligibility to a federal radiation program.
The diffusion plant, also known as PORTS, was shut down in 2001 due to contamination and environmental concerns , but residents said they’re still paying the price.
Judge approves competency evaluations for 2 adults in Ohio child abuse case Wendy Carrier grew up about five miles away from the first U.S.-owned uranium enrichment production operation. Her grandfather, uncle and father all worked there.
“He would come home and take showers before he would let us get on him or play with him and not that that helped anything because the radiation was already there,” Carrier said.
Her father died in 2017 after a battle with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Now, she is undergoing chemotherapy for a lymphoma with no cure. According to the American Cancer Society, radiation exposure is linked to a higher risk of cancer.
“It’s devastating to see all our friends and families just losing people left and right to cancer,” Carrier said.
PORTS workers received some compensation after the plant shut down but help for impacted families was never included.
Northeast Columbus property with deceased owner, criminal history boarded up “It just makes me mad to think that there are so many people going through this and they don’t have the financial stability to do anything,” Carrier said.
The new bill, if passed, would expand the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act and open up eligibility to residents like Carrier.
“I’m asking for enough money to get through this cancer treatment and be able to live comfortably,” she said.
Carrier is a single mother of two and said the help would be life changing.
“I want them to be kids. I don’t want them to have to have jobs so we can pay bills,” she said.
